facts.statement: Theiophytalia was a herbivorous iguanodontian dinosaur that lived in Colorado, USA, during the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 112 million years ago.
facts.quote: Theiophytalia is a genus of herbivorous iguanodontian dinosaur from the lower Cretaceous period (Aptian-Albian stage, about 112 million years ago) of Colorado, USA.

facts.statement: A partial ornithopod skull was discovered in 1878 by James Kerr at Garden of the Gods park in El Paso County, Colorado.
facts.quote: In 1878, a student of Colorado College named James Kerr found a partial ornithopod skull at Garden of the Gods park in El Paso County, Colorado.

facts.statement: The fossil skull, cataloged as YPM 1887, was originally identified by O.C. Marsh in 1886 and later affirmed by Gilmore in 1909 as belonging to the species Camptosaurus amplus.
facts.quote: The skull, YPM 1887, was referred by O.C. Marsh (affirmed by Gilmore, 1909), to whom the skull was given in 1886, as that of Camptosaurus amplus.

facts.statement: Microscopic analysis revealed the skull came from the Lytle Member of the Purgatoire Formation, confirming it was Early Cretaceous in age rather than from the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: However, microscopic comparisons of thin-sections of the Mesozoic formations in the Garden of the Gods showed that the specimen actually came from the Lytle Member of the Purgatoire Formation; therefore, the skull was Early Cretaceous in age.

facts.statement: The genus name Theiophytalia is derived from the Greek words for "divine" and "garden" or "garden of the gods".
facts.quote: The generic name is, from Greek, θειος, theios: "divine" + Greek φυταλία, phytalia: "garden", or "garden of the gods".

facts.statement: The species name kerri honors James Hutchinson Kerr, the discoverer of the specimen.
facts.quote: The specific name kerri honors James Hutchinson Kerr, who found the specimen.

facts.statement: The skull found in 1878 at Garden of the Gods park in Colorado Springs is the only known fossil of the genus Theiophytalia.
facts.quote: Garden of the Gods is a park in Colorado Springs, Colorado, where a skull, the only fossil of the genus yet to be discovered, was found in 1878.

facts.statement: The original description classified Theiophytalia as an intermediate form in derivation between Camptosaurus and Iguanodon.
facts.quote: The article describing the find classified Theiophytalia as intermediate in derivation between Camptosaurus and Iguanodon.

facts.statement: Cladistic analyses from 2010 and 2011 recovered Theiophytalia as a basal member of Styracosterna, with Hippodraco identified as its closest relative.
facts.quote: In 2010 and 2011 cladistic analyses of McDonald and colleagues, Theiophytalia has been recovered as a basal member of the Styracosterna and its closest relative was Hippodraco.

facts.statement: Theiophytalia belongs to the parent group Styracosterna.
Theiophytalia is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
Theiophytalia lived between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago, spanning the Aptian to Albian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Albian (121.4 to 100.5 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Comparisons by Brill and Carpenter (2006) showed the skull had a longer, heavier, and more rugose snout, a wider dorsal process on the maxilla, a proportionally smaller antorbital fenestra, and a stouter quadrate with a bulbous lower jaw articulation.
rejected.quote: Detailed comparisons by Brill and Carpenter (2006) also showed that the skull differed in a number of key features from that of Camptosaurus, namely: a longer, heavier, and more rugose snout; a wider dorsal process on the maxilla; a proportionally smaller antorbital fenestra; and stouter quadrate, with a bulbous articulation for the lower jaw.
